big: Rohan owns 10 shares at ₹1,000 each, worth ₹10,000. The company announces a split. Next morning he owns 20 shares at ₹500 each. He is not richer, and he is not poorer.

lines: The company split its shares. Should I be excited?
A split cuts the same pie into more slices. The price per share falls and the number of shares rises. Your total value is unchanged on the day.

alt: Bars showing shares doubling, price halving and total value staying the same after a split
caps: After a 1-to-2 split, he has 20 shares.
The price per share halves to ₹500.
His total value stays ₹10,000. Nothing was created.

intro: What each one does to you.
rows: A company sells shares to the public for the first time
A share of profit, decided by the board, never guaranteed
More shares at a lower price, same total value
Extra shares from reserves, price adjusts down
note: Bonus 1 for 2: 10 shares become 15, and the price drops by a third. Total value stays about the same.

q: A company announces a 1-to-5 split. Meena has 10 shares at ₹1,000. What does she have after?
why: That would be a reverse of a split, where the price goes up.
The price must fall as shares rise, or value would be created from nothing.
A split raises the count of shares. It does not cut it.
Five shares for each one gives 50, and the price falls to a fifth, ₹200.

q: A company has a good year. What is true about its dividend?
opts: It must be paid every year by law
The board decides, with no guarantee
It is a fixed rate set by SEBI
It is paid only to new buyers
why: No law forces a company to pay a dividend each year.
The board decides on a dividend, and it can change or stop.
SEBI does not set a dividend rate for companies.
A dividend goes to the holders on the register, not only to new buyers.

q: A company gives a bonus of 1 share for every 2 held. Rohan has 10. How many does he hold after?
why: 12 would be a bonus of one for every five held.
20 would be a bonus of one for every one held.
One for every two on 10 shares gives 5 more, so 15 in all.
5 is just the bonus and leaves out the 10 he already holds.

opts: A first sale of shares to the public
A bank pays interest on a deposit
A sale of old shares by a broker
A new rule from SEBI on brokerage
why: An initial public offering is the first sale of shares to the public.
Bank interest is about deposits, and has no link to an IPO.
Trades in listed shares between investors are not an IPO.
A rule on brokerage is a regulation and not an IPO.

pts: A split gives more shares at a lower price. Total value is unchanged.
A bonus issue gives extra shares from reserves, and the price adjusts.
A dividend is decided by the board and is never guaranteed.
